analysis.one_liner: Keeps in-home aides for seniors exempt from minimum wage and overtime pay rules.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have spared home care agencies from paying their aides minimum wage and overtime, never received a hearing or vote after being introduced in October 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would write into law a broad exemption from federal minimum wage and overtime rules for people providing in-home companionship and personal care to seniors and people with disabilities. Crucially, it would extend that exemption to aides employed by home care agencies rather than directly by families, and it would strip the Labor Secretary's authority to narrow the exemption through regulation. Sponsors pitched it as a way to keep home care affordable, but its direct effect is to leave agency-employed aides without a federal wage floor or overtime pay.
analysis.who_benefits: Home care agencies and staffing firms that employ aides as third-party employers would be spared federal minimum wage and overtime obligations, their largest cost. Families paying for care could benefit if agencies pass the savings along as lower prices, but nothing in the bill requires or even encourages that.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Home care agencies and staffing firms

how_it_helps.text: The bill extends the Fair Labor Standards Act's companionship services exemption — no minimum wage, no overtime — to third-party employment, meaning aides employed by an agency rather than directly by the family would stay exempt, even when working for multiple households in the same week.

It strikes the phrase tying the exemption to definitions 'by regulations of the Secretary,' which would remove the Labor Secretary's power to narrow the exemption by rule — exactly the power used to extend wage protections to agency-employed aides.
Live-in domestic workers employed through an agency would remain exempt from overtime requirements, not just from the reach of families who hire them directly.

analysis.who_pays: Agency-employed home care aides — a workforce that is largely women and often immigrants — would remain outside federal minimum wage and overtime protections, able to work 60-hour weeks with no overtime premium and, in principle, pay below the federal minimum. Any benefit to families depends entirely on agencies choosing to pass cost savings through.

drawbacks.text: The bill would guarantee that aides hired through agencies — the fastest-growing part of the home care workforce — can work long weeks with no overtime pay and no federal minimum wage floor, and Congress would lock that in so no future Labor Secretary could restore the protections by regulation.

The affordability argument is indirect: the bill controls agencies' labor costs but contains no requirement that agencies lower prices for families, so the savings could simply stay with the employer.

Defining 'companionship services' to include help with bathing, medication reminders, and incontinence care sweeps in work that is essentially caregiving, not mere companionship, blurring the line the exemption was historically built on (only care requiring trained medical personnel stays covered).

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's stated benefit — keeping home care affordable for seniors and families — is speculative, since nothing in the text requires agencies to pass labor savings to customers. The costs are concrete and fall on a low-wage, predominantly female and immigrant workforce that would lose the federal wage floor and overtime protections that had just been extended to them. An honest supporter would have to concede that this is primarily a labor-cost bill for the industry, with family affordability as a hoped-for side effect.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in late October 2015 and sent to the Senate labor committee, which never held a hearing or vote on it before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Pat Roberts introduced the bill on October 29, 2015, joined by 13 Republican cosponsors, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee.
The committee took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote appear in the action history — and the bill died when the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.
Because the bill died, the Labor Department's 2015 rules extending minimum wage and overtime to agency-employed home care aides remained in place.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Home care aides came out ahead: the wage and overtime protections that had been extended to agency-employed workers stayed in force, and agencies did not get the statutory exemption they sought. The bill's sponsors gained nothing from its failure.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Home care aides kept their wage protections

for.name: Sen. Pat Roberts
for.what_they_did: Sponsored and introduced the bill on October 29, 2015.

for.name: 13 of 54 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, including Sen. Lamar Alexander, chair of the committee it was referred to.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled.

against.name: Obama administration Department of Labor
against.what_they_did: Its 2015 rule extended minimum wage and overtime protections to home care workers employed by third parties — the change this bill was written to undo — so the bill's failure preserved that rule.

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes on the bill; all 14 supporters at introduction were Republicans (14 of 54 Senate Republicans) and no Democrat signed on, but no one ever had to vote on it.

industries.industry: Home care agencies and staffing firms
industries.note: The bill's core move is extending the minimum wage and overtime exemption to third-party employment — i.e., to agency-employed aides — which removes the industry's biggest regulatory cost from the 2015 Labor Department rule. Its gain comes directly out of its workers' pay.

industries.industry: Home care and domestic workers (aides, CNAs, nannies, housekeepers)
industries.note: These workers are the bill's direct cost-bearers: the bill defines them broadly as 'domestic service' employees and keeps them outside federal minimum wage and overtime protections even when an agency employs them. They are ordinary workers, and their loss is the public's loss.

Sponsors argue cheaper labor keeps care affordable for seniors and families, and lower agency costs could translate into lower prices — but the bill contains no mechanism requiring agencies to pass savings on, so any benefit is indirect and uncertain.
